newsitem.title: USA: Daschle urges compromise on disaster bill.
newsitem.headline: Daschle urges compromise on disaster bill.

text.p: Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle Wednesday urged his Republican counterparts to drop two add-ons to a disaster relief bill vetoed by President Clinton, saying flood victims should not be held hostage by politics.

"There are many ways with which to address this issue," Daschle, of South Dakota, told NBC's "Today" show after congressional Democrats held an all-night gabfest Tuesday to urge Republicans to come up with a strategy to respond to Clinton's veto.
"We can compromise and we will find a way with which to resolve the census issue and the continuing resolution and the other extraneous matters.
"We don't like holding people hostage for extraneous issues that have nothing to do with providing disaster assistance."
Clinton vetoed the $8.6 billion money bill because it contained provisions to prevent a government shutdown and require traditional person-by-person census counts.

During a Tuesday evening House session, the Republicans rebuffed 216-205 an effort by Democrats to pass the $8.6 billion money bill without the controversial provisions despite appeals from Upper Midwest lawmakers whose states have yet to recover from ravaging spring floods.

Democrats responded by taking their case for swift approval of disaster relief funds directly to the public Tuesday in a 12-hour all-night talkathon that featured multiple live interviews and online chat.
Billed as an "all-night vigil," the back-to-back television and radio interviews and live America Online conversations took place in Daschle's suite of offices just off the Senate floor.
Daschle, when asked what he thought would be the public's reaction to the politicized atmosphere of the bill, said: "I think that in many cases it is petty and ineffective.

"What we're hoping is that they all appreciate the fact that Congress isn't just one individual, it's 535 people, some of whom have vehement disagreements with what the Republicans are trying to do here."
NBC said it invited Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi and House Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia, but the two Republican leaders declined to appear.
